blocks.x: Richard McLean You can give your name. My name is Richard McLean.
Do you have any middle initial or middle name?
Well, I have a middle initial, but it's very seldom used. In other words, I forget about it. That initial is A, but very seldom anybody ever...
Is your son's name Richard too?
No, my oldest son... The one that plays guitar? I did have a son named Richard, but he died long years ago. And this boy I have now, my oldest boy now, his name is Ernest.
Ernest, the one that plays guitar?
The one that plays guitar.
Well, just where were you born? Do you remember the street about where it was?

Well, I'll tell you the truth. I don't know exactly what street, but it was up in the uptown section on the other side of the Port United. My mother always told me that I was born somewhere on a street called Waters Street. Waters Street. And that Waters Street would be one block on the other side of... on the front of town side of Chaptula.
Oh yes. Yeah. The river kept changing up there.
Yeah, around Jenna and Waters. I remember my mother telling me that's where I was. And what was the date? The date was January 25th, 1898. 1898.
Long time.
That's not so bad.
What did you do?
Well, in the early days, my early days, I never thought too much about music. You know, that is... Did your father or mother play any instrument?
Anybody in the family play?

Well, my mother didn't play any musical instrument, but my mother had a nice voice. In other words, she sang in the choir, the church she had belonged to. And that was a church... It's right at the corner of Cades and Coliseum right now. It's called St. Peter's Church.
Is that a Baptist?

No, that's a Methodist church. Methodist church. Methodist church. Well, outside of that, I don't know if anybody else outside of my son that's a musician, of course I had an uncle with a fine song too. Okay. Yeah, I have a picture of him right now.
Did he work professionally as a singer ever, as an imitator?

No, but he sang what you call glee clubs. Oh, yeah. He was in his church up there in Chicago. I told you, I just told you I had a picture of him right now. I'd like to show it to you before you go. Yes, I would like it.
If you have any other pictures of some of the bands you played in, I'd like to see those too. What's your name?

Well, when I was around the age, when I got around 16 years old, I had a, I used to go around with boys, most of my friends, you know, they had a few that played piano. And one boy I remember with a fine violin playing. In other words, he could play most any of the string instruments. Yes. The guitar, the violin, and the mandolin. You see? And I would be with these boys so often, till a lot of people thought I could play, although they never saw me with instruments, you know? You see? So, one day somebody asked me, say, you always with these boys, why don't you play some musical instruments? You see? So, I said, well, I never did give it a thought. So, I don't know, all of a sudden I went to a friend, Bob of mine. He played drums. His name was, we always call him Neneet, but his name was Bryant. You might have heard of that name. I don't believe so. He was from, he went to Chicago a long time ago. So, I told him, I said, Bryant. Bryant. Bryant. Bryant. Bryant. I can't think of his first name. I always said Neneet Bryant, you see? But anyway, I told him, I said, I think I'm going to buy me a mandolin. He said, I want to play a mandolin. He said, well, mandolin is a nice instrument. He said, but since you're going to learn how to play an instrument, why don't you learn something that you can make a few dollars with? I said, well, what's that? He said, get a guitar, man. He said, guitars? They use guitars in bands. They don't use no mandolin in bands. I said, well, yeah, that is a good artist. So, I did buy a guitar. I sent away for a guitar.
How old were you then?

I was about 16, 16 or 17 years old. So, I bought the guitar. And after I got the guitar, I didn't know what to do with it. And as far as for guitar teachers, they were scarce. A lot of fellas, they played the guitar. They said, well, I'll show you what I know, but you'll see them today. Maybe they wouldn't see them no more for the next two, three weeks or a month.
You see?

So, I kind of give up on that guitar. I'll just let it stay there. I got it in a big box. You see? And just the way that box come, I set that guitar around in there. I didn't see that guitar in the morning for about two years. I went away. I went to Chicago and I stayed in Chicago about two years. I come back from Chicago and I was working out at a lumberyard called Otis Lumberyard. And it rained one day out there and the weather was cold. And they knocked us off from work, you see? And I come on home. And I got home. There was nobody living in the house between me and my mother. When my mother was working, well, that left me being in the house by myself. So, I made me a big fire. This stone, in the old time greats they call it. Oh, yeah. Made me a big fire and I just sit down there like that. And the only light in the room was the light from the fire. So, I had been sitting down there reading a magazine and I'd been read it so many times. I almost knew it by heart. I thought it in the corner. And I happened to look over and I saw the guitar. I hadn't put my hand on that guitar in about two years, like I told you. I went and I got the guitar and I pulled it out of the box. And when I pulled it out of the box, I kind of tilted the box. When I tilted the box, a little book fell out of there. And inside of there they had something else in there. I didn't know it was in there. You've never seen that. They had a little tuning. They had what you call a tuning fork. Yeah. They had that in there. So, I looked at it and I saw letters on there, you see. So, I thought, I said, well, what is this for? So, then I began to read the book. Well, the book tells me what it's for. That's the sound of each string. So, I took the guitar out and I blowed that and I tuned up the string. And this little book was a diagram book. It shows you where to put your fingers out, you see. So, I sit down there and I figured out how that should be done. But, you know, just doing it by myself, I didn't know if it was right or not. Well, I got the guitar in tune, but I didn't know it was in tune. So, there was a friend of mine, about two days after that, he asked me about the guitar. He said, don't you have a guitar? I said, yeah. He said, well, what, are you learning how to play it? I said, well, no, I don't. He said, well, if you don't learn how to play, why don't you sell it to me? He said, I need a guitar. I told him, I said, well, all right, come take a look at it. So, he picked up the guitar and he strummed it, you know. He said, well, who tuned it up? He said, well, I was a bit surprised, you know. I said, it's in tune? He said, yes. I said, well, I tuned it up. He said, well, I thought you said you couldn't play. He said, well, I can't play. So, he wanted to buy the guitar for me. He said, how much you want from me? I said, well, I didn't say I wanted to sell it. I said, but if you want to buy it, I'll sell it to you for six dollars. He said, well, okay. He said, I'll give you a dollar and a half now and I'll give you a dollar and a half Saturday. I said, well, I don't want to sell it like that. Okay. Well, he said to me, he said, well, you want to learn how to play? He said, I'll help you out with it. All right. Well, by not selling that guitar to him, if he had maybe had six dollars to give me, I probably wouldn't have been playing music today. You see? But he gave me a few ideas on to get drunk and I just began to build them up. Build them up. And I'd get around some places where these friends of mine played piano and I'd strum behind them until I began to get an ear for changing chords. And I just kept on going like that.
Yeah.

And a little while after that, I met my wife and I kind of let that go again. Yeah. You see? And after I got married, I stopped going to this place and all around like that. I had a little more time in the house. So in the evening, I would sit down and strum on the guitar when I come from work. You see? And playing on the guitar, I was passing and would hear me, but I didn't know he was listening to me. You see? I didn't realize anybody was paying any attention to me playing on the guitar. Where did you live in those days?
About?
Well, I was living right, at that time I was living right here on St. Philo Street between Roman and Prayer. That's right.
That's right.

That's right. That's right. Yeah. So one day it was a Halloween day. It was Halloween. And the fella came by there and asked about the fella that he heard playing guitar. Well, that was me. You see? Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. house I was in then. So by this fella hearing me, he knew Artie Boyer, he come back asking for Artie Boyer. So my wife's aunt said, well he don't live here anymore. He said, well, I thought I heard him today when I passed here. She said, well, we didn't hear him because he hadn't been here in quite a while. She said, well, I'm sure I heard a guitar playing, somebody playing a guitar in here. Oh, she said, well, maybe you heard my niece's husband. So he said, well, is he there? He said, no, he said, why? He said, well, I'd like to get him to play with me tonight. So she rang up and asked for me where I worked at, you see. And they told her I wasn't there. Well, I was on my way home then. I used to come home for lunch every day on the account of my wife being sick at the time. You see, I'd come home every day on that account. So when I got there, my wife's aunt told me, she said, there's a musician coming out and he said he wanted to, how you play with him tonight? Oh, I said, I want to play with him. I don't know how to play. I never played with a band before in my life. I said, I don't want to play with him. She said, well, I'm going to tell him to come back because he left a dollar deposit here for you. I told her, I said, we got nothing to do with that. She said, well, you better go because if you don't, she kind of calls herself frightened, you know. She said, you better go because you got this man's dollar and he can put you in jail. So, and then I said, well, I had to take up, I took up the noise. I said, well, I'll go. That was your first job. That was your first job. That was pretty good. So the man, he came back. He said, tell him to meet me at Claiborne and St. Philip. So I guess the fellas, knowing maybe somebody I'd never saw before in his life, he probably wouldn't know where I was. He came to the house to meet me. You see, instead of me meeting him at this corner right here, he comes to the house. When he come to the house, we went and walked in all together. So he said, what's your name? I said, man, Richard. Who used to play with Richard? I said, no. So I said, well, I'll try right, you'll make out. So I went off and I played.
You got along all right?
I got along all right. So the big thing came off is when he had to go, huh?
Who was the fellow? What was the name of the band?

I don't remember. Up until the day, I don't remember. The only thing I remember about him, he was a bass player. He was a tall, tall dogfella. But I always, in all these years, I always tried to find out the man's name, but the way I describe him to people, nobody seems to know who I'm talking about. You see? And so, I'll finish to tell you that. The big thing came off when he said, well, it was time to pay me off. So when the man got ready to pay me off, he had, what seemed to have nothing but one dollar bills in his hands, you know? So he said, well, I didn't pay, I said, all right, come on, go ahead and get your money. So he started to pay me off. He handed me a dollar, and he handed me another dollar, and he handed me another dollar, you know? Couldn't believe it. So after he got up to about three dollars, I started to draw my hands back. He said, come on, get your money. So he handed me another dollar. You see? And every time he'd hand me a dollar, I'd draw back. So he'd hand me another dollar. So he kept on handing me until he had handed me seven dollars, you know? So he handed me seven dollars. I just stood up and looked, and just froze, you know? I couldn't move. So he said, come on, man, put your hand money in your pocket and let's go. Man, my pocket, you might not believe it, but I was holding money all the way.
Man, my pocket, you can't get your hand money in your pocket.

That's the truth. So when I got home that night, the party we had played, the people had fixed sandwiches and everything that we could take home. And I got home. Well, everybody knew I was in there because it looked like the door wasn't big enough for me to get in there, you see? So when I got there, I told my wife, I said, look here. She said, what's that? I said, look what that man played me for playing tonight. So we just sit down there and just spread the money out. Like a big sheet, just stood up and look at it.
You didn't even want to take the job.

Get out of here. I didn't want to take the job. So after that, some of the fellas I played with that night, they began to hire me, playing, you know? And I've been just going out like that and making the jobs like that. And that was on the guitar I was playing. Then after a while, things began to drop off. I hardly saw any of those fellas, you know? And then there was a boy, his name was Victor Spencer. You ever heard of Victor Spencer?
I remember.

He was a trumpet player. And he hired me to play several jobs, you know? So one day, one of the boys in the band told me it was John Kasmer. He said, man, he said, Vic gonna fire you. I said, what? He said, man, Vic want a banjo player. He's gonna get a banjo playing his band. He said, you don't play banjo, you play guitar. I said, yeah, well, that's right. I wasn't too particular, you know, I wasn't too worried about it. I was working and I said, well, I wasn't worried about it anymore. So my wife said to me one day, she said, what's the matter? You stopped playing music? I said, well, the fellas don't hurt me no more because they're using the banjo. And I said, tenor banjo. I said, I don't know how to play tenor banjo. She said to me, well, if you learn how to play the guitar, you can learn how to play the tenor banjo. I said, yeah, that's true, true. But who's gonna teach me how to play a banjo? She said, well, just look around for a teacher. I said, well, yeah, that's the idea, right enough. So I went on out and I bought a banjo.
That was the Vega? That was the Vega banjo.
No, that was an Orpian banjo, it was called. Orpian banjo. So I bought that banjo and after I got that banjo, there was a trumpet player, his name was White, Amos White.
Oh, yes, I know him.
I know him, yeah.
California now. Yeah.

He had heard me playing several times on the guitar and he'd come along and he asked me what I play with. I told him, yeah, I said, well, I reached for the guitar, it'd come to my house. He said, no, bring the banjo. I said, well, I can't play the banjo. I said, I'm learning how to play, but I can't play. He said, well, I'll tell you what to do. He said, you know how you tune the first four strings on your guitar? I said, yeah. He said, you tune your banjo just like that. Yeah. He said, the only thing you don't have is the two big strings, the A and the string. He said, you understand that? I said, yeah. He said, well, all right, get your banjo. Let's try it out right now. So the banjo being so sharp and respond so much, it looked like it gave me more life, you know? So he said, well, you see that? I said, yeah. He said, well, come on. He said, but don't, don't take it for granted that that's the way you're going to play it. He said, you try to learn the right, the right tuning. He said, yeah. So soon enough, I went on and I played a whole lot of jobs with him. Like that. Him and Lee Collins, which happened to be in that band, another boy named, what was his name, his name? Cindy Correll. You ever heard of Cindy Correll? Yeah. Cindy Correll. I've heard of him. I've heard of him. That was some of the band. I'm telling you now, Cindy Correll, White, Lee Collins, and Freddie Babu. And the drum player was Joe Lindsey. Joe Lindsey. Joe Lindsey. That was the drum player. And the bass player, the only one I can't remember. I played with that band. We went all in the little country town of the spring.
Ever worked many jobs here?
In that band?
I mean, that wasn't the band that was played up at the Astoria. Lee Collins played up there.
The entertainers. No, no, no. That was the, that was the, that was one, you know, in the early part of my band. That was before that, those days.
Yeah.

So, well, after, after I left that band, then I started playing with my wife's uncle. His name was, uh, Onall the Pass. Oh, yes. You heard him? Drummer. Yeah, that's right. Never knew him, but I've heard of him. Well, he had, his band was called, he called his band Olympia Band. You see? I played with him just about four months. And one night I went over to a place called, I think they call it the E-Light at that time, it was a cabaret. They used to call them cabaret or cabaret, something like that. Is that one on Ramparm Street? No, this was on, uh, on, uh, Iberville between, uh, Bugunda and Ramport. Yeah. Right along, almost where the, the post office is right now. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Well, I happened to go over there that night, Sam Morgan had a benefit dance over there. And I went in there. And they had different bands would come in and fellas would come in and play, this is like what you call jam sessions. And I don't know. Any musician in the place, they would ask me to sit in and play a few now. But the fellas didn't know me too good, especially those fellas that were in there, like Sam Morgan, and Joe Renner and, and, uh, a few others I could name. Well, the ones, the, the, the few that knew me, well, they'd ask me to play. They'd say, come on, you, you're the only one that haven't played anything. I said, come on and play. Well, I went and played and there was, uh, a boy, uh, that was playing at that time, his, uh, the banjo there, his name was Thomas. Everybody called him Son Thomas. Oh yes, I've heard of him. So Son said to me, say, come on and, come on and play, rest me up, man. So I said, on and up. Yeah. So Joe Renner was playing drama at the time. Kid Renner, right? Yes, yes.
I've seen him.

Yeah. So, uh, that night went on, but I didn't know what that night would mean. That would mean to me in the later years, you know. So, about a couple of months after that, uh, my wife's uncle, in all the past, said to me, he said, I heard Renner is looking for you, just like that. Kid Renner. Kid Renner. I said, well, Renner don't even, I said, Renner don't even know me. I don't know. He said, but that's what I heard. All right. So I didn't pay too much attention to that. But one day, I'm sitting on my step in the same black, right there on the first street. And I had my oldest boy, the boy that died. He was just about two years old. And I was sitting down on the step. It was a winter day, but the weather was warm and the sun was shining. I was sitting in the sun at the top. I saw Renner coming down the street, him and another fellow. And, uh, he come down the street and he stopped at my wife's uncle's house, the house I used to live in. The house knocked on the gate. I was on the side. Well, I knew Renner, but Renner didn't know me, you see. So I called over to him and I said to him, I said, I said, you're looking for a no? He said, no. He said, yes. He said, yes and then no too. He said, but I'm looking for a banjo player that lives around here named Richard. He said, yeah.
Yeah.

So I told him, I said, well, my name is Richard. He said, you play banjo? I said, yeah. He said, well, you must be the one I'm looking for. He crossed the street. So he said to me, he said, did you play over at Eli one night over there?
I said, well, I sit in and on a fella's place.

He said, well, you the one I'm talking about. He said, I'd like to hire you for Saturday night. I said, well, I have a job for Saturday night. So he said, well, how about Sunday night? Well, I said, well, yeah, that'd be all right. So he said, well, I'll tell you, you'll be at the economy hall for quarter to eight. I said, okay. Well, I had heard about Randy's band. It was a nice band he had. And I had heard his band too. You see? And I couldn't hardly realize he'd come to hire me to play in his band even one night. He'd come to the stage, you know? So I told him, all right. So I don't know what, what the buildup I had got with him and what, but Randy come to my house that Sunday morning. He was playing up in a little place called Lulin. He used to play up there every Saturday night. And he left right for me and then come to my house. He'd tell me to be sure and be after he got me off. So I told him, no way, I'll be there. Randy seemed not to be too sure about, I don't know if he thought I would come or not.
Yeah, he's having to worry about it.

He come to my house about 6.30 that Sunday evening. Good catch. He said, remember old man Glennie? You know old man Glennie? Sure. Yeah, old man Glennie was with me because the old man Glennie played that same job. So I went on off, I played the job that night. And after I had played about four or five numbers, the trombone player was named Morris French. Morris French come over to me and says, to me he said, you're going to stay with the band? I said, you're going to stay with the band? I said, I tell him, I said, well I'm only hired for the night. He said, well man, he said, you want to play with the band? I said, well, that's left of Randy. I don't know. He said. Randy said to Morris, I said, don't worry about him, I'll take care of him. He said, well, I'm going to stay with the band. So after the night was over, and they said to me, he said, you did fine. He said, did much better than I expected. He said, that's why I wouldn't, I wouldn't tell you anything else. He said, but I want, I would like to keep you in my band. What you going to play? Oh, I said, yeah. And I was, I was, I was doing this all the time. So he said, well, all right, then he said, I'm going to give you the list. He gave me the list of his dates.
Yeah.
Now he gave me all of the dates he had, and Mardi Gras was just about two weeks off.
He was really busy.

And when I looked at that list he had, he had every night up to Mardi Gras. And I had just, it was about 12 or 13 dates on that list he gave. I went on, I played with Rainier from that time. It was about 19, 1923, I think. It was 23.
Did you keep your day job or give it up then later when you started working so much?

Well, I happened not to be working then. I had a job, but it was a part-time job. I was pressing, real pressing shop. And I only worked three days a week. And that was on the corner of Royal and Espanol.
I was going to ask a little bit more about Arno De Pass. Is it De Pass or De Pass? It's D-E. D-E, De Pass. Was that called the Olympia or Young Olympia Band?
No, he called his band Olympia.
Olympia. Because I know one time people tell me Freddie Keppard had a band with.
Well, that's where he took the name from. That's from Freddie Keppard.
Did Ricard Alexis play trumpet with you at that time? I think he told me he played once in the Young Olympia Band or something.

Ricard? No. He wasn't looking at it. No, no. I'll tell you. He was the trumpet, do you remember? In that band, well, I'll tell you. When I was playing in his band, he had, let's see. Shots was playing. Shots. Because Shots played trumpet for a while, you see. Now, I can't remember if he had anybody else after that. But I know he had shots. Henry Julian was the saxophone player. And, and, well, I forget a lot of, I forget a lot of those people. Boy, is that one?
Yeah, it's hard to remember all those names.

See, but I didn't play with him too long. I couldn't, I think, I don't think I played with him all over four months. And in that four months, the kind of band he had, well, it was, the band wasn't playing as often as bands like Randy's band. No, no. So in that four months time, I played, four months time, I don't think I played over ten jobs.
That's it.
You see, and sometimes he probably had a different man, you know, playing.
Was there another brother of Arnold in the past that played music? Somebody who was very good. Mm-hm.
Dave DePass you say was the clarinet player?

Clarinet player, yeah. Now his other half brothers was Rudolf Bollier and Octave, Octave, a fair few old people say I pronounce it Octave Bollier. Well after leaving René's band, then I went and played with Sam Morgan's band.
Ask a little bit more about René's band, who his clarinet player was? Could you tell us?

When I first went in the band, the clarinet player was Zeb, you call him, but what does Zeb, do you know his last name? I know his name but I just can't think of him. Most people don't even know, they just say Zeb until they know. I'll tell you who knows his name and remember his name, it's Happy. Yeah. And Joe René, his brother, the drum player. You said Morris French was the drummer. Morris French. I mean the trombone. Yeah, Morris French. Now his bass, the bass players, when I first went in the band, he had lost his, one of his good bass players, that was Sam Maria. And at that time he was using old man Grenny, when I first went in the band.
He had, was it Marrero?
No, Simon Marrero. Simon. Yeah, that was Sam. Maybe it was the old man Billy, it wasn't the old man, Simon. No, no, Simon. Simon was before, just before I went in the band.
Yeah, I see.

And he was, at one time he had Bob French playing, Bob French played tuba with him for a while. And Albert Morgan played with him, Albert Morgan played with him for a while, but not very long when I was in the band. And another bass player he had was Bob Lyons played with him for a while, while I was in the band. See, so I stayed in that band a good while. You see? And one time his clarinet player was, uh, Louie, Big Olly Louie. Yeah, Louie stayed in the band about one year. Louie was, Big Olly Louie was in the band when we won that cup up at La Ola.
Well, what was that? No, I heard about something.
I think that was in 1925.
Can you tell me some more about it? I forget.
Well, we played against Kid Punch up there. Oh. Punch. That's the band we played against, and Louie was in that band then.
And Loyola University, a college dance?
Yeah. And they, you know.
How did they decide? Did people vote or clap for it or committed to decide? Who was the judge?
Well, I think it was committed. It wasn't no applause or nothing like that. I think it was committed, you see? I think that's the way it was decided.
Did they judge by all night long or just play a couple of pieces for the contest?
No, we played the whole night. The two bands played the whole night, you see. And after, you know, after it was over with, then the couple decided who it was for. I had the cup here.
It stayed here about, I had it here about two years.
And Miss Renee came and got it just, you know what I mean? She let me keep it.
Oh, well, I think of it. Do you know Joe Renee's address? I've, I saw him years ago.
No, I don't know Joe's address. I don't know his address. But, uh, I know his, I know Renee's wife's address and she might could tell you.

Yeah, she'd probably know too. If you have it in your mind, you can just say it now and we'll have it on the tape and we can check on it. Or else I'll look it up later. Yeah. I'd like to talk to his wife. But you mean, uh, Miss Renee's? Yes, uh, Mrs. Mary.

Well, my wife, my wife could tell you right now her address. We'll get it done after a while. Yeah. Well, anyway, after I left, after I left, after I left, I went to, uh, Sam Morgan's band. But I was just working in somebody else's place. I wasn't supposed to be in my place, but I played with his band one year. Sam Morgan's. You see. I played one night club called, they call it the Humming Boys. Oh yeah. George Gaynor told me about that place. Well, I, I, I take George's place in there. George, uh, uh, uh, got shot in the leg accidentally, you see. And they put me in here. I played, went and played in his place for a while. See, but I left from there. That's the place George Gaynor was playing in. And when in another place, the same people open up, call it, and they call it the Humming Boys. Now, we, uh, in that plane, we had a boy named Henry Jury and played saxophone and the same guy was playing drum then, played drums. That's right. And, and, uh, uh, what you call them, uh, uh, Joe Robichaux was playing piano, you see. And, uh, the trumpet player, let's see, who was the trumpet player? I don't know if it was, I don't know if it was. That's right, somebody else can tell us. Well, after Henry Julian left, we had, uh, uh, Colbert, Jim Colbert playing saxophone, and, and, uh, Albert de Conje playing trumpet. And the, and the rest of the fellas, you know, I gave cards to myself. I was playing banjoling, you see. And I left from there and went on the music box playing the banjol. You heard of the music box?
I'm not sure, no.
Well, that's, the music box is right on the corner where Stein's closing store is now.
Oh, yeah, down on Canal. That's right, Stein, that's what, uh.

In Carondelet. Yeah, Carondelet. Canal and Carondelet. I went up there playing with Eddie Jackson. I know you heard of Eddie Jackson. Oh, yeah, bass player, yeah. Yeah. Well, we had, up there with Eddie Jackson, that's when I went up there and, uh, I found, I found octave up there. Octave was playing piano up there.
Was that one of the, uh, dime dance, uh, taxi dance halls, or? That's what it was, yeah.

You see, cause, Octave left the hummingbird before me. So that made, when I get over to the music box, I find octave over there playing piano. You see? And they had Eddie Jackson out there, Henry, uh, Oscar Henry, Tron, uh, uh, uh, George McCollum, trumpet. Uh huh. And the same Henry Jury playing saxophone. Uh huh. Then, then that's the piano. What was the drum? Was playing drum at the time. Uh huh. And, of course, they changed, changing a few men. They had, they had, uh, an arm of twiar. One time played trumpet up there and, and a boy named Joe Stratus played drum. And, uh, little, little Lester Santiago. Oh yeah. He took, uh, Octave's place up there on piano. You see? Well, after I left from the music box, George McCollum had come back in the band. You see? And, when we left the music box, we, they, uh, George got together a band and we went over at a place called, uh, Alamo. Oh yeah. That was a dance hall, too. Uh huh. And we stayed over there quite a while. You see? When we left the Alamo, we come on, I come on out from there and I, I just played around then with different bands, you see?
You see?

Uh, it's hard to tell who I played with. Yeah. I wouldn't play with that, just to remember. But one of the bands I got in after that was one of the bands that always feel that the best band I ever played with. That was the Sonny South band.
Whose band was that?

Sonny South? That was the band that Eddie Pearson played in, Cindy Monagirl, uh, another boy named, uh, uh, Elliot Taylor, Emile Fritz, uh, Booker, uh, Booker, uh, uh, uh, uh, play Sousa for him, uh, uh, uh, in bass violin. What is book is?
Well this is, uh, Fritz, excuse me for interrupting, uh, uh, what was his name, Fritz?
What did he play? Yeah, he played tenor saxophone. Tenor saxophone. Yeah, you tell, he played the clarinet.

I was gonna ask him more about, do you remember, uh, where he came from? George Lewis tells me about a wonderful clarinet player, Isidore Fritz, across in Mandeville, across the lake. Do you think he was any relative? No, I don't think so.
No. Is he still living?
Emil Fritz? Yeah.

But I don't, I don't, uh, he, he don't play anymore. Maybe we'll find him though, I'd like to talk to him sometimes. Yeah, well, uh, I, I tell you where you, I know where you, I know where you can find him, I don't know where he live at. Yeah. But at the, at the Autocrats Club? Oh yes, around the Autocrats. He's, he's, he's there very near every day or every night, you see. They try to find him there. Well, that band, the Sonny Shots band, well that was a big band.
Who was the leader? Did they have a leader?

We had, uh, uh, oh, what's the boy's name? Uh, McNeil's name was almost like mine and I could have, could have hardly remember. McNeil, Albert McNeil. He was the trumpet, one of the trumpet players. You see, and the other trumpet player was, uh, uh, uh, how did, not how did they, did they know? Leo, did they know? That was the other trumpet player. Yeah. The other band, the band had trombone, three saxophones. The other saxophone player was, uh, was, uh, George Johnson.
It always got little cards, let's, let's get that on here. Okay. What kind of a card is it? You don't have those down in our part of the city. No.

Yeah, well, after leaving that, after, after coming out of the sunny south band, well, I was, uh, telling the truth, it seemed like it was curtains for me cause I, I didn't care, I didn't worry about, too much about playing with it. And it was during depression at that time too. Yeah. That would be bad too. Whenever I get a job, it'd be a job paying about a dollar, a dollar and a half, you know. Uh huh. It was really worth that. It wasn't worrying about it too much. So I had no family. I had to do something. Well, I would go from place to place, you know, maybe pressing and working in pressing places, you know, all like that to get along. Then, uh, finally I found myself in, in what you call a WPA. Uh huh. Used to WPA at that time. And, and,
They banjo, uh, in the band up there?

Yeah, I, after, after I'd worked, I'd done worked all around here, you know, digging mud and everything. You see, so, they, when they met, they, when the band was up there, they told me, they said, Now, why don't you try to get in that band? Yeah. So I did. And I got in the band. You see. I got in that band, well, I was doing, I was doing much better in a way because the band, the band, paid more, more, more money and the fellas was working out there and all that
money. What did they pay at WPA?
Uh, uh, let's see, what would we make? We make, we make in around 19 something, we make, we amount to about $19 a week.
A week. Well, I guess in those days things were cheap, you could live on that.

Yeah. So, uh, after, after getting out of that band, it's when the war, you know, when the war was beginning there in full room, man, I, uh, went on and my brother-in-law, and we all call him Cuckoo, but his name is, uh, Todd.
Oh, he's your brother, he was your brother.

You know, we, I say brother-in-law, but his, his, uh, uh, my, my sister-in-law's husband, in other words. Yes. Well, you say brother-in-law. Yes, I understand, that's right. Yeah. He opened up a little place up on, uh, Ramport Street, cleaning and pressing, laundry. I knew he'd been up there.
You see?

Well, I, I knew a little about the work already, see, so I went right on up there, went to work. And I did all this, the linen clothes, you know, shirts and all the linen clothes. And I stood up there and worked good well. And I, I, I even turned down jobs. You stayed there? I mean, uh, uh, uh, working places where, they wanted me to work over there regularly. On, uh, Iperville Street when they had that little nightclub, and I wouldn't go over there. I said, well, I'm doing all right where I'm at. You see? I stayed right there. I worked with them. And then finally, Cindy Delivine came along, and, and he, in other words, he picked me out of the mob bars, you see. And I went on, I played with Cindy Delivine for two years. Still on banjo?
On, on, no, guitar.

Well, guitar again by that time. And, uh, when, while I was up there is when I bought the bass. See, I always could play some on the bass, but I never did play jobs on the bass, see. So I did, I went, I bought a bass. So I had the bass about, I had the bass about 18 months. So this, uh, uh, boy just passed, uh, Howard, kid Howard? Yes. He said to me, he said, man, I heard you, you got a bass. I said, yes, but I can't play it. He said, oh, I know better than that. He said, I got to have a bass player. I said, I want you to play it. I said, well, if you can stand it, so can I. He said, well, I'll tell you what you do. He said, I have a little part at my house. He said, why don't you come on out with the bass? He said, I'll give you a chance to play it out a little bit. I said, all right, there's one center, you ran the next block and went on over there. And I played over there. And the fellas that, the fellas I played with, they never said one word about me playing the bass. It seemed like it was just something they already heard me playing.
About what year was that? Around 1940 or during the Depression?
That was about 44.

Mm-hmm. So, right after that, I had played with Howard quite a while. And I played the bass with another boy named, uh, we always called him Don Raymond. See, I played with him and he had a big band, you see. Well, playing with him, it gave me a chance to get more acquainted with the bass because he did have music, you see. He used to play a lot of fun music, you see.
I forgot to ask you, when you learned to read music, did you work that out by yourself? Or some of these people helped you, like, uh, the guitar? Well, that's something I forgot.

That was one thing I forgot to tell you. Well, I first, you see, when I first started playing with him, I was just playing by ear, what's it called. Well, after I began to play with these bands, some of these bands used to use music, you see. And playing with those bands, they would play pieces that, I mean, my ear just wasn't good enough to catch the chords, you see. So, uh, uh, I said, well, I'm gonna try to learn something about the music anyhow, so I'll be able to make the right chords. So, I went to John Morell. You heard of John Morell? Yeah. I asked him to teach me, he said, well, sure, I'll teach you. So, I went to John once, and the next time, every time I'd go to his house, his wife would tell me, well, John is in Paschettan. She said, he's in Mobile. Yeah. I never could catch him on. So, this-
Was he with Celestan in those days, I guess? Who's that? Was he with Celestan?

That's right, that's who he was playing with. So, there was a violin player, I heard about it, I said, well, I thought violin players would know something about any string instrument. That's the way I thought it anyway.
Yeah, you think so?

I went to a fellow named Correll, that's the same, Cindy Correll's brother. His brother was a violin player. His name was George. I went up there to him, he said, well, I'm gonna tell you, he said, banjo, that's a funny instrument. He said, why don't you learn how to play some other instrument, and then you can figure out how to play that banjo by me. I said, well, what instrument would you suggest? He said, well, I don't know. What you think you'd like to play? I said, well, I always just like to play. I always wanted to play a clarinet. So, I went and bought a clarinet. I paid $15 for clarinet, this foe was named Bean. I bought the clarinet for him. I think he got hurt by an automobile and he died. His name was John. He was a real old drummer, old-time drummer, John Dean. I think his name was Cindy too, Cindy Bean. Well, anyway, I got the clarinet and I went to a fellow man, his name was Caguleta. I think his kind of little Caguleta. And I took five lessons from him. And I took five lessons from him, I just felt I had enough lessons. And from then on, I learned how to play banjo, the chords. The music. The chords from the music. I could play, I could almost play them upside down. That's the truth.
People tell me you were a wonderful banjo player. That's the truth.

I could almost play the chords upside down. You turn the page upside down. I could still play and I was still reading the music. Do you still play your banjo very much? Well, I don't play too much, no. My fingers seem to be weak. I played it the other night when I went to Baltimore. That's when I played. Oh, in Baltimore you're good at that again. Yeah. Well, that's how I learned the little music I know. That's how I learned. I put the clarinet down and it stayed down. I didn't bother about it anymore.
You still have your clarinet?
I have, it's not the same one, but I do have a clarinet. Is it the Albert system? No, the one I have now. The band? The band system.
The new system.
Yeah, that's right.
Most of them use the Albert here.

Yeah, well the first one I had was the Albert. And I could play a lot on it. I played enough to play a job, the job was right there. Oh, you did. And that's something very few people know. That's right. Very few people know that. That's true. So, anyway, after, after...
Talk about playing with Kid Howard there for a while and then you played bass.

Yeah, when I left I played with this boy I was talking about, Don Ramon. Well, I didn't play too long with him. But finally, Paul Barbaran, he gets in the jam for bass playing. You see, Stuart Davis was playing bass with him and he had a job going out of town. You see? Yeah. And Stuart didn't want to go. We could find a bass player right away and Albert Walters told him, he said, well why don't you get Richard? Because he had heard me play with Howard, you see? So, Paul told him, he said, well Richard plays, I want a bass player man. He said, I want Richard to play the guitar. So, I was told him, he said, man, Richard's playing bass. He said, well, Paul rang me up at four o'clock in the morning and asked me to play. And he asked me to play. I refused the job because I had spread in this ankle and it was swollen up like this. You see? So, I explained to him why. He said, well man, you don't have to, we'll take care of the bass and everything for you. You won't have to care or nothing. You see? And we'd be playing at it. He said, well get a high stool for you to sit on. He said, come on, make the job. I got to have somebody. He said, the job's paying $20 a night.
Good luck.
So, I said, well all right then. And I went on off with Paul.
You see?
Playing with him. Well after, well I began to be a member of Paul's band then.
You see?

Then after Paul slowed down a little bit, he wasn't doing too much in the music. You see? Then George Williams, he happened to come along when Lloyd was playing the bass. And he wanted me to play with him. So, I played with George Goodwell. I played with George about three years, three years. Longer than that. Then finally here come Paul back again. And that's when you saw me out there on Boydville Street. You see? When I was with Paul. That's when he come back for me the next time. You see? And leaving Paul has come right where I am today. Yeah.
How long have you been with Bill Matthews now?

Well I started over there in 55. 55? Four years. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But with all of that, not being too much of a musician, I did teach boys how to play. My son happened to be one. Cindy Gates was my first one.
What was that?

Cindy Gates, yeah. And there's the other two boys, they're very fine guitar players. There's one Trevene and two of them. One is Oivin Trevene and the other one is Curtis Trevene. I taught them. Well there's a few other boys, there's a few others I won't even mention their names because they seem to tell other people, you didn't show me anything. Yeah, sometimes there's a certain jealousy. So when I found out Oivin, I just won't mention the name of them. No, I don't either. And that's true.

A lot of people have told me how wonderful you were on banjo, like Professor Mineta, and we just stopped at George Gaynos, he said you could play some banjo. They all talk about it, so I wish I could have heard you sometime. I never always think of you as a bass player. Which instrument do you really enjoy most, bass or banjo, guitar?
I'll tell you, I'll tell you. Player of that, maybe. I don't know why I didn't have a bass long years ago because I always did like the bass.
That's your favorite then today?

Yeah, I always did like the bass player. I remember long years ago I used to listen at the bass players and they used to use the bowl then, you see. I would sit down and listen at the music and to me I didn't hear anything else but the bass. My mind would be on it so much, you see. And that's just the way when I'd be sitting down and listening at any band or player, the first thing my ears would fall on is the bass. I mean that was even before I played the instrument. And even Perez, I'd go to hear Perez. To me I'd go there more to hear the bass playing than anything else. And Eddie Jackson was one of my favorites.
Did he play string bass a good deal too? I knew he was a famous tuba player.
Eddie Jackson played the string bass but not too much. You know what I mean? He seemed to didn't care too much about it either. But he was wonderful in that too.
In the brass bands he was. I never heard him but everybody told me that.
Gee, if you were him, if you just, I wish you would have had an opportunity to hear him. He was one of the most powerfulest men I ever heard on that instrument and he had what you call this ear.
He could really play it I think.
And you could tell him from anybody. You could tell his playing from anybody else on the street. That's right. It just looked like it was something made for him to play. It was made for him to play.
That's right.
That was my son just came in.

Yes, we'll try to talk to him. We have a couple more minutes here. We might as well finish up this reel. I could ask you a few things like about your instruments. I noticed you have this King bass here at home. What kind of a bass do you have over at the paddock on the job?
What make you remember? The bass I have at the paddock is an Epiphone bass.
Epiphone.

Yeah, and I'm telling the truth between the two instruments, you know. This one has got a nice sound already now, but the other bass is the Epiphone is more powerful. I had this bass on the job shelf at the time. And I don't know if the people out there could help, but me playing it myself, I can hardly hear myself with this bass. I imagine playing with a band that plays softwares.
I'm going to ask what you think about these new fancy electric basses they have.
Have you seen or heard any of those? Well, I've heard them, but I never had a chance to play with them.
What about electric guitar? Did you ever play electric guitar or just the usual?
Oh yeah, that's what I played when I went out. You had the electric attachment? Mm-hmm, that's what I played when I was playing with Senior Desvene.
Yeah, I didn't know if you used the electrical amplifier on it.
Yeah, that's what I was playing with him.
Do you really, do you have to have that electric to be heard nowadays, you think, in the band, or can you still hit it hard enough to play your thing?

Well, I'll tell you, the while I, when I was playing with Senior Desvene, I had an electric guitar. It was a big band. Built in. Yeah. What you call an electric guitar. But after playing with him a while, I bought a, what you call a straight guitar. You know it? And that was an epicophone guitar too. I have it upstairs now, but my son, he broke it. And I used to use that with a pickup. You understand? Yes. Now the only time I would turn that, when I wouldn't be playing a solo, you see, a feature chorus. I'd turn that completely off. And you could still hear it, even though he had the band, a good sized band, twelve pieces. That's what you call it. But you still could hear it. You see, and I would, I'd much rather play it like that. You know, with that electric turn completely off and play it like that because I could play it the way I was used to playing. I like that sound better myself. Yeah, you see, you know, because electric guitar, you go ahead and the power's just beating on them like that, they start to hooping like wow, wow, wow, wow. You see? Somehow it's a bad time. But having, just turning that off, just turning that completely off and being an instrument like it is, you know, just playing nothing inside there to mute it. Well I just could sit down there and play it just like the old time players.
Hit it good and hard and get some real rhythm in there.

Yeah, you just play it, you see? And of course the way, our way up playing long years ago, you know, we'd make all kind of different strokes on the instruments, you know? And you, on an electric guitar, it would sound bad. You see, it would just sound like you're just taking something and just rubbing it on something, wah, wah, wah, wah, wah, like that. Yeah, just a big rumble of noise sometimes. Yeah, you see? What about this banjo, Mr. McClain? Yeah, I'm going to ask what the, what make this is?

That's some, ah, bacon? This is a, it's a bacon banjo, you see? Because I'm not familiar with that, it's a very fine looking instrument and it has that mute on it too. Yeah. Let's see if you can see the note. Oh, there you want. Yeah. See, see, see the note. Oh, there you want. Yeah. See, see the note. Oh, there you want.
Yeah. See, see the note. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. See, see here. See, see here. See here. Bacon. Yeah. See right there. Can you see it? Not too well, but.
Bacon and I can't see what else.
B-A-B-A-C-O-N, bacon, and it looks like a couple more letters or something. Yeah. Well, that's telling where, that's, uh, uh. Connecticut. Yeah. Bruton, Connecticut. Yeah. Bruton, Connecticut.
Connecticut. Yes, a very nice inlay. It's a resonator.
This banjo is called Montana.
That's the name of the model, the particular model. Yeah.

Well, uh, uh, during the time of Waterville days, at the Palace Theatre, used to have Waterville shows coming on here. Yeah. And, uh, they had a, uh, uh, uh, uh, banjo player. His name was Bill, Montana. You see? And he came down dressed like a cowboy in white, in white, in white. His hat and every clothes and everything was white. And the banjo he played, you see, was all white. And this is supposed to be one of the models. That's all you see. Oh, yeah. Yeah, Montana model. Yeah, Montana. They named that banjo after him. Montana.
It's, uh, it's got a nice tone to it, doesn't it?
Yeah. How do you, um, how do you play it when you, how do you operate it when you've got your
mute? Do you press it on your knee?

Well, uh, you see, when we, when I'm playing, you used to sit, of course, I'd be sitting in a different position. Better chair than them. And now. And, uh, I keep my foot on my toes, my you know, right on the tip of my toes so I can raise up like that. Oh, I see. Yeah. You see? I can't so well do it now because I'm kind of out of practice, you know? But really I could play a piece.

segments.title: Interview opening: name and son Ernest
segments.summary: McLean gives his name and middle initial and says his oldest living son Ernest plays guitar.

segments.title: Birth in uptown New Orleans, 1898
segments.summary: He was born January 25, 1898, on Waters Street by his mother's account.

segments.title: Music in the family
segments.summary: His mother sang in St. Peter's church choir and an uncle sang in glee clubs in Chicago.

segments.title: Deciding to buy a guitar at sixteen
segments.summary: Friends play instruments; a drummer friend steers him to guitar, and he sends away for one but finds no teachers.

segments.title: Teaching himself guitar from the tuning fork and book
segments.summary: After two years in Chicago he finds the diagram book and tuning fork in the guitar box and tunes it himself; a friend wants to buy it.

segments.title: First job playing guitar on Halloween
segments.summary: Married and playing at home, he is hired on a deposit dollar to play with an unnamed bass player's band.

segments.title: Paid seven one-dollar bills
segments.summary: Paid at the end of the night in seven dollar bills, he lays the money out for his wife.

segments.title: Victor Spencer's band and switching to banjo
segments.summary: Playing guitar for trumpeter Victor Spencer, he learns Spencer wants a banjo player and buys a tenor banjo.

segments.title: Learning banjo with Amos White's band
segments.summary: Amos White shows him how to tune the banjo; he plays country jobs with White, Lee Collins and others.

segments.title: Arnold DePass's band and sitting in at a benefit dance
segments.summary: He plays with his wife's uncle Arnold DePass, then sits in at Sam Morgan's benefit dance where Kid Rena hears him.

segments.title: Kid Rena comes looking for him
segments.summary: Rena comes to his house looking for the banjo player who sat in and offers a Sunday night job.

segments.title: First night and permanent job with Rena's band
segments.summary: After his trial night at Economy Hall Rena hands him a list of dates through Mardi Gras and he joins in 1923.

segments.title: His day job at the pressing shop
segments.summary: He worked part-time pressing clothes three days a week.

segments.title: Arnold DePass's Olympia Band and its players
segments.summary: Discussion of the Olympia name from Keppard, its musicians Shots and Henry Julian, and the few jobs he played.

segments.title: DePass family members
segments.summary: Dave DePass was the clarinet player; half-brothers named Bollier are mentioned before he moves on to Sam Morgan.

segments.title: Musicians in Rena's band
segments.summary: Clarinet, trombone and bass players who passed through Rena's band while he was in it.

segments.title: Band contest against Kid Punch at Loyola
segments.summary: Rena's band won a cup in a night-long contest against Punch Miller's band, judged by a committee.

segments.title: Looking for Joe Rena's address
segments.summary: The interviewer asks for Joe Rena's or his wife's address.

segments.chapter: Other New Orleans clubs and bands
segments.title: Sam Morgan's band and the Hummingbird
segments.summary: He plays a year with Sam Morgan's band and fills in for George Guesnon at the Hummingbird club.

segments.chapter: Other New Orleans clubs and bands
segments.title: The Music Box and the Alamo
segments.summary: He plays banjo at the Music Box taxi dance hall with Eddie Jackson and then at the Alamo dance hall.

segments.chapter: Other New Orleans clubs and bands
segments.title: Sonny South band, his favourite
segments.summary: The Sonny South band is the best he ever played with; he lists its large personnel.

segments.title: Depression years and the WPA band
segments.summary: Work dried up in the Depression; he joined the WPA band, earning about nineteen dollars a week.

segments.title: Cleaning shop work and Sidney Desvigne
segments.summary: During the war he worked at his brother-in-law's cleaning shop until Sidney Desvigne hired him for two years on guitar.

segments.title: Buying a bass and playing with Kid Howard
segments.summary: He buys a bass, is invited by Kid Howard to try it, and then plays with a big band.

segments.title: Learning to read music and trying the clarinet
segments.summary: He sought teachers, took five clarinet lessons and learned chords from music.

segments.title: Joining Paul Barbarin's band
segments.summary: Recruited at short notice to play bass for Paul Barbarin, later playing three years with George Williams.

segments.title: Present job and teaching guitar
segments.summary: He has been in his current band since 1955 and has taught young guitarists.

segments.title: Why the bass is his favourite instrument
segments.summary: He always listened first to the bass and likes it best.

segments.title: Eddie Jackson's bass playing
segments.summary: He praises Eddie Jackson's powerful, distinctive playing.

segments.title: Comparing his basses
segments.summary: A King bass at home and an Epiphone he uses on the job, which is more powerful.

segments.title: Electric guitar and amplification
segments.summary: Views on electric basses and guitars, and how he played an Epiphone guitar with a pickup with Desvigne.

segments.title: The Bacon Montana banjo
segments.summary: Examination of his Bacon banjo, the Montana model named for a vaudeville player, and playing it with the mute.
